titre: The Golden Ratio No One Has Actually Measured in the Parthenon
accroche: Pyramid, Parthenon, Mona Lisa: the golden ratio is said to be everywhere, except in the real measurements of the buildings and paintings.
contenu_vulgarise:
The golden ratio, φ = (1+√5)/2 ≈ 1.618, is the proportion most often invoked in talk about beauty: it is said to be carved into the Great Pyramid of Giza, to organize the façade of the Parthenon, to lie hidden in the Mona Lisa's face, and to turn up in the proportions of the human body. The trouble is that, measurement after measurement, these claims do not hold up.

## What the Measurements Actually Show

The Great Pyramid lost its outer casing in antiquity, which makes its original edges impossible to recover with enough precision to settle between several competing numerical theories: φ, π, or simple integer ratios all fit the remaining measurements about equally well. The historian Roger Herz-Fischler showed, in 2000, that the “Kepler triangle” theory (in which φ would appear in the slope of the faces) assumes a level of mathematics that the Egyptians of the Old Kingdom did not possess, and that no Egyptian written source mentions this proportion.

The Parthenon fares no better. The American mathematician George Markowsky, in a 1992 article that remains the reference on the question, went through the common claims one by one and checked them against the actual architectural surveys. The researcher Keith Devlin sums it up: the claim that the Parthenon was built on the golden rectangle is not supported by the actual measurements. A 2014 study, covering fifteen temples, eighteen monumental tombs, and some sixty funerary stelae from fifth-century-BCE Greece, simply finds no trace of the golden ratio in classical Greek architecture.

## Where the Legend Comes From

Markowsky traces the myth back to its roots: ancient Greek mathematicians, Euclid foremost among them, did study the properties of this proportion, but nothing in their work, nor in Vitruvius a century before our era, connects that study to any theory of beauty. The link between φ and aesthetics is forged much later, carried through the twentieth century by writers who go looking, after the fact, for this proportion wherever it can roughly be made to fit, and it fits often, because a rectangle whose sides are in a ratio close to 1.6 is nothing exceptional among the proportions a human eye finds pleasing. On the Great Pyramid, Markowsky states it plainly: it does not appear that the Egyptians even knew of the existence of φ, much less incorporated it in their buildings.

The golden ratio remains a perfectly real mathematical object, with elegant, provable properties. What does not hold up is its extension into a universal aesthetic that the ancients supposedly sought out on purpose: that part of the myth was manufactured after the monuments, not before them.

carte.punch: Pyramid, Parthenon, Mona Lisa: the golden ratio is said to be everywhere, except in the real measurements.
carte.idee: The Great Pyramid, the Parthenon, and the Mona Lisa are routinely said to be built on the golden ratio. Archaeological surveys and a landmark 1992 study show the opposite: no ancient source mentions this proportion, and the real measurements do not confirm it.

quiz.question: What does Roger Herz-Fischler's 2000 study show about the theory that the Great Pyramid follows the golden ratio?
choix: That it relies on a level of mathematics the Egyptians of the Old Kingdom did not possess, and that no Egyptian written source mentions this proportion
That it is accurate, measurements in hand, and that the golden ratio does govern the slope of the faces of the pyramid
That it comes from a written decree of the pharaoh Khufu, found sealed in the burial chamber
That it was invented outright by Markowsky himself for the sake of his own argument
quiz.explication: Herz-Fischler shows that the Kepler triangle theory assumes mathematics unknown to the Old Kingdom, and that no Egyptian text mentions φ; the missing edges, due to the lost outer casing, also make the measurement itself uncertain, which has nothing to do with a decree or an invention by Markowsky.
